chapters.title: Chapter 2: Computing a Company's Taxable Income

lessons.title: Deductible and Disallowed Expenses: What the Tax Law Lets You Claim

body.text: An expense is deductible when it is spent wholly and exclusively for the business, is not capital in nature, is not personal, and is not something the law has specifically blocked. Four tests. Almost every dispute with an assessing officer is about one of them.

children.text: The last lesson showed the bridge from book profit to taxable income. This one goes line by line down the profit and loss account and asks which costs survive. Get this right and your computation has almost nothing added back. Get it wrong and you pay tax on money you have already spent.

Section 34 [old 37(1)] is the workhorse. It allows any expenditure laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business, as long as it is not capital or personal in nature, and then carves out three things by name: spending for a purpose that is an offence or prohibited by law, CSR spending, and political advertisements.

body.caption: The four questions every expense has to pass

cells: Business purpose
Was this spent wholly and exclusively for the business?
The founder's holiday, a family wedding, a personal insurance premium
Revenue, not capital
Is this a running cost, or did it create a lasting asset?
Buying a machine, adding a floor to the factory, acquiring a trademark
Not blocked by name
Has the law specifically refused this?
Penalties, CSR spending, political advertisements, income tax itself
Conditions met
Was TDS handled, payment mode correct, amount reasonable?
No TDS deducted, cash above the daily limit, an inflated payment to a relative

body.text: Capital expenditure is not lost. It is recovered slowly, through depreciation under section 33 [old 32], across the life of the asset. Only the timing changes. Revenue expenditure hits your tax bill this year, capital expenditure over several years. That distinction is what most of this lesson's grey areas are really about.

body.caption: Everyday business costs that are deductible, with the conditions attached

cells: Salaries, wages, bonus and commission to employees
Yes
TDS on salary must be deducted and deposited. Bonus and commission are allowed only when actually paid, under section 37 [old 43B]
Rent, municipal rates, repairs and insurance for business premises
Yes, under section 28 [old 30]
TDS on rent above the threshold. Repairs must be current repairs, not an upgrade
Interest on money borrowed for the business
Yes, under section 32 [old 36(1)(iii)]
Interest to banks and NBFCs is allowed only on actual payment under section 37 [old 43B]. Borrowings must genuinely fund the business
Professional fees, audit fees, software subscriptions, marketing
Yes
TDS where applicable, and the cost must be revenue rather than the build of a lasting asset
Bad debts actually written off
Yes, once written off in the books
A provision for doubtful debts is not enough. The debt must have been offered as income earlier
Employer contributions to provident fund and gratuity funds
Yes, for recognised and approved funds
Employees' own contributions must be deposited by their due date or the deduction is lost
GST, cess and other statutory dues
Yes
Only if paid before the return due date under section 263 [old 139]
Travel, freight, power, security and other running costs
Yes
Cash payments above ₹10,000 to one person in a day are disallowed in full

body.caption: Costs that get added back, and how much

cells: Penalties and fines for breaking any law
All of it
Section 34 [old 37(1)] excludes spending for an offence or prohibited purpose
CSR spending under the Companies Act
All of it
Named exclusion in section 34, even though the spending is legally mandatory
Political advertisements
All of it
Named exclusion in section 34
Income tax, surcharge and cess
All of it
Tax on profit is an appropriation of profit, not a cost of earning it
Payments to residents without deducting or depositing TDS
30% of the expense
Section 35 [old 40]. Restored in the year the TDS is finally paid
Cash payment above ₹10,000 to one person in a day
The entire payment, not just the excess
The limit is ₹35,000 for payments to transporters
Excessive payments to relatives and related concerns
The excessive portion
Old section 40A(2) lets the officer compare against fair market value
Personal expenses of the owner or directors
The personal portion
Fails the wholly and exclusively test in section 34
Provisions and estimates, such as doubtful debts or warranties
All of it until it becomes real
A timing difference, allowed when the loss actually crystallises

stats.label: Cash payment limit
stats.context: Per person, per day. Cross it and the whole payment is disallowed

stats.label: TDS default
stats.context: Of the expense, added back until the TDS is deposited

stats.label: Penalty or CSR spend
stats.context: Added back permanently, with no later year to look forward to

body.title: Try It: Total the Add-Backs
body.prompt: A trading company's profit and loss account includes: ₹40,00,000 salaries with TDS deposited on time, ₹12,00,000 office rent with TDS deducted, a ₹1,00,000 penalty for a labour law violation, a ₹25,000 purchase paid in cash to one supplier in a single day, ₹3,00,000 of CSR spending, and ₹6,00,000 of interest on a working capital loan, fully paid during the year. What is the total amount added back? Answer in ₹ lakh.
body.explanation: The penalty of ₹1,00,000 and CSR spending of ₹3,00,000 are both fully disallowed, and the ₹25,000 cash purchase is disallowed in full because it breached the ₹10,000 daily limit. That is ₹4,25,000. The salaries, rent and interest all survive, because TDS was handled and the interest was actually paid during the year. Note that the cash payment loses the whole ₹25,000, not just the ₹15,000 above the limit.

children.text: Repair or Improvement: The Line That Moves Money Between Years

The capital versus revenue question has no formula. The test used in practice is whether the spending merely keeps an existing asset working, or whether it creates something new, extends the asset's life, or increases its capacity.

body.title: Same factory, two kinds of spending

columns.label: Revenue: claim it fully this year
points: Replacing a worn belt or motor in an existing machine
Annual software subscription and maintenance contracts
Rent paid for machinery taken on hire

columns.label: Capital: claim it slowly, through depreciation
points: Adding a new floor or a new shed
A one-time ERP implementation that creates a lasting system
Acquiring a trademark, licence or goodwill
Major overhaul that materially extends a machine's life

body.title: Quick Check: This Year or Over Several?
body.question: A Faridabad manufacturer spends ₹8,00,000 during the year. Which of these is deductible in full this year?
options: ₹8,00,000 to install a second production line
₹8,00,000 to replace the roof sheets and repaint the existing shed
₹8,00,000 to acquire a competitor's brand name
body.explanation: Repairs and repainting keep an existing asset in working condition, so they are revenue expenditure and fully deductible this year. A new production line, a van and a brand name are all capital: they are recovered through depreciation under section 33 [old 32] over several years. The money is not lost in any of those cases, just claimed more slowly.

children.text: In a company owned and run by the same family, the boundary between business spending and personal spending gets blurry fast. Assessing officers know exactly where to look.

body.title: Scenario: The Consultant Nobody Can Describe
body.scenario: A Delhi trading company pays the founder's spouse ₹18,00,000 a year as a marketing consultant. There is no written contract, no deliverables on file, and the spouse has no marketing background. The company also claims the full running cost and depreciation of a car that the founder's family uses at weekends, and pays ₹4,00,000 a year in rent for a floor of the founder's own house that stores inventory.
body.prompt: Which of these three claims will survive scrutiny, and what would make them safer?
body.modelAnswer: All three are defensible in principle, but only if the paperwork matches reality. The consultancy fee is the weakest: payments to a related person can be disallowed to the extent they exceed fair market value, and with no contract, no deliverables and no relevant background, an officer can treat most of the ₹18,00,000 as excessive. Fix it with a written agreement, a scope of work, evidence of the work done, TDS deducted, and a fee that a stranger with that skill set would command. The car fails the wholly and exclusively test to the extent of personal use, so the company should either keep a usage log and claim only the business share, or treat private use as a perquisite in the director's hands and tax it there. The rent is the cleanest of the three if the space is genuinely used for inventory: keep a rent agreement, deduct TDS on the rent, pay by bank transfer, and be able to show the stock stored there. The pattern is consistent. The tax law does not object to paying family members or using owner-owned assets. It objects to claims that no independent evidence supports.

body.text: Two traps hide inside employee costs. First, the employee's own share of provident fund, deducted from their salary, must be deposited by the due date under the PF law. Miss that date and the deduction is gone permanently, unlike the employer's share, which follows the gentler payment rule in section 37 [old 43B]. Second, bonus and commission are deductible only when actually paid, so a bonus declared in March and paid in September falls into the next year unless it is settled before the return is filed.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Cash Rule
body.textWithBlank: When a business pays one person more than ₹10,000 in cash in a single day for an expense, the amount disallowed is ___ of that payment.
body.explanation: The entire payment is disallowed, not merely the part above ₹10,000. Splitting one bill into several cash payments across the same day does not help either, because the limit applies to the total paid to one person in one day. The limit is ₹35,000 where the payment is to a transporter for hiring or leasing goods carriages.

body.title: Startup founders: three costs people always ask about

children.text: Incorporation and preliminary expenses: costs of setting the company up are not ordinary business expenditure, because the business did not exist yet. The law allows them to be written off over several years instead of all at once.

Fundraising costs: legal and due diligence fees for raising equity are generally capital in nature, tied to the share issue rather than to running the business. Fees for arranging a business loan sit on the other side of the line and are usually deductible.

Customer discounts and cashbacks: genuine discounts reduce revenue or count as marketing spend and are deductible. Keep the commercial rationale documented, because large discount and cashback claims in consumer businesses draw questions.

body.label: The rule behind every rule in this lesson
body.context: A contract, an invoice, a bank transfer and a TDS challan turn a claim into a deduction. Without them, an honest expense can still be added back.

body.title: A Monthly Discipline That Protects Your Deductions
steps: Pay every material expense by bank transfer, and keep cash payments to one person under ₹10,000 a day
Run a TDS check before any vendor payment is approved, not after the year ends
Keep a written contract for every payment to a relative, director or related company, and benchmark the amount
Tag capital spending separately in the accounting system so it is not buried inside repairs
Deposit employees' provident fund share by its own due date, every month, without exception
Settle bonus, commission and statutory dues before the return filing date under section 263 [old 139]
Review the expense ledger once a quarter for anything personal that has slipped in

cards.definition: The general deduction rule: expenditure wholly and exclusively for the business, not capital or personal, and not an offence, CSR or political advertisement.
Other specific deductions, including interest on capital borrowed for the business and bonus or commission paid to employees.
Rent, rates, taxes, current repairs and insurance for buildings used in the business.
A running cost that keeps the business going, deductible in full in the year it is incurred.
Spending that creates or improves a lasting asset, recovered through depreciation under section 33 [old 32].
Work that keeps an existing asset in working condition, as opposed to an upgrade that extends its life or capacity.
The benchmark used to disallow the excessive portion of a payment made to a relative or related concern.

points: Section 34 [old 37(1)] allows expenditure that is wholly and exclusively for the business, not capital, not personal, and not specifically blocked
CSR spending, political advertisements, penalties and income tax are disallowed by name, and never come back
Capital spending is not lost, only claimed slowly through depreciation under section 33 [old 32]
A cash payment above ₹10,000 to one person in a day is disallowed in full, not just the excess
Failing to deduct or deposit TDS costs you 30% of the expense until the TDS is paid
Payments to family and related concerns are allowed at fair value, with contracts, evidence and TDS to back them up
Deductions are won on paperwork: contracts, bank transfers, invoices and challans

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax advice. Section references reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 as understood at the time of writing, with the corresponding 1961 Act section shown in brackets. Limits, rates and provisions change with each Union Budget, and the capital versus revenue question often turns on the specific facts. Consult a qualified chartered accountant on borderline items before claiming them.
